title: Domain Attributes Hidden Behind Tuple or Array Positions
pattern: A structured domain record is represented by an unnamed primitive tuple/array, or conceptually different attributes are grouped in a homogeneous indexed container merely because their storage types match.
why_bad: Readers must remember the index-to-meaning mapping (e.g., which string is the city vs. the state, "index 0 is width, index 1 is height"), that knowledge spreads across every consumer, and changes to positional layout can silently break same-typed values or index accesses because the compiler cannot detect swapped fields of the same type.
detection: Identify (a) primitive tuple aliases used as domain definitions, whether the elements are mixed-type or equal-typed, and (b) literal tuple/array index reads (e.g., `tuple.0`, `arr[1]`) used to recover distinct semantic fields from a homogeneous container. In both subcases, establish that the elements are separate attributes rather than a genuinely uniform mathematical sequence.
counterexample:
Conventional vectors and coordinates with uniform mathematical behavior and a standard dimension ordering (e.g., $(x, y, z)$ coordinates) are legitimate positional representations:
```rust
let point_2d: (f64, f64) = (10.0, 20.0);
```
source: *Domain Modeling made Functional* by Scott Wlaschin (p. 75); *Practical Object-oriented Design* (p. 84); Sandi Metz *POODR*, Chapter 2: "Obscuring References", p. 24.
